messages.author: ebac19664dad3407
messages.subject: Nonlinear model with discontinuous gradient
parts:
I have a student who's looking at rice yields in Sri Lanka. For N villages, she has records of the amount of irrigation water applied to the fields in each village for each year and the rice harvest. Different villages were established in different years, so some have longer records than others.

She wants to model the rice yield as a function of water. The expected functional relationship is

rice[i,j] = max(0, alpha[i] * (1 - exp( - beta[i] * (water[i,j] - gamma[i]))))

where rice[i,j] is the rice harvest for village i in year j (in tons per hectare), water[i,j] is the water (in millimeters) applied to the fields during the growing season, and alpha, beta, and gamma are parameters (all greater than zero) that characterize, respectively, the maximum yield, the water-use efficiency, and the minimum required water. If you supply less water than gamma, your plants die and you get no rice. If you supply more than gamma, then the rice harvest increases with water, asymptotically approaching alpha when the water is much greater than gamma. We are studying drought and water scarcity, so in many years water is close enough to gamma that we can't ignore it.

The goal of the analysis is to find alpha, beta, and gamma for each village, with estimates of their uncertainty. These numbers will then be used in an econometric analysis of the marginal value of changing the supply of water for irrigation.

I'm not sure yet how I want to model the noise (the stochastic variation in rice from year to year if water is held constant). The amount of rice has to be greater than or equal to zero, so I could add noise drawn from a distribution before applying the max(0, ...) function but maybe there's a more efficient way to do it.

My student fit the parameters alpha, beta, and gamma for each village individually, using a canned gradient search function in Matlab, but some of the villages have short records and never get enough water to clearly observe the asymptote at alpha, so the fits are not well constrained.  After reading Phil's post at Andrew's blog "Everything I need to know about Bayesian statistics, I learned in eight schools" I'm thinking that this is a lot like his radon in Minnesota problem and it would be better to model the data together, using a hierarchical treatment of inter-village variation in alpha, beta, and gamma by drawing each village's parameters from a parent distribution, so the villages with lots of data and lots of variation in water can help constrain alpha on the villages with short records and/or little variation in water.

However, I am new to MCMC analysis and have some trepidation at diving into Stan with a model that's both nonlinear and not continuously differentiable (as the note at the beginning of section 29.5 in the manual warns). Is this problem just too pathological, or is it reasonable to try Stan?

I am working on coding a model using rstan and generating synthetic data with known alpha, beta, and gamma to see whether I can recover the parameters, but I'm new to this and slow, so I figured that I would ask the experts for advice in parallel with trying to figure it out on my own.

Thanks for any advice anyone has for me.

Jonathan Gilligan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonlinear model with discontinuous gradient
parts:
On 2/13/14, 8:09 AM, Jonathan Gilligan wrote:
> I have a student who's looking at rice yields in Sri Lanka. For /N/ villages, she has records of the amount of

> irrigation water applied to the fields in each village for each year and the rice harvest. Different villages were
> established in different years, so some have longer records than others.
>
> She wants to model the rice yield as a function of water. The expected functional relationship is
>
> |
> rice[i,j] = max(0, alpha[i] * (1 - exp( - beta[i] * (water[i,j] - gamma[i])))||)
> |

This will be problematic for Stan if the right-hand operand of max
is < 0, because then you lose gradients contributed by
rice[i,j] and water[i,j] for alpha[i], beta[i] and gamma[i]. If that's
not expected to happen, it won't be a problem.

You're going to see correlation among alpha, beta and gamma due to the
form of the expression, so I'd suggest a covariance-based hierarchical model
for them, which then techncially should be on the log scale because they're
positive-constrained:

(alpha_log[i], beta_log[i], gamma_log[i]) ~ multi_normal(mu_abg, Sigma_abg);

alpha <- exp(alpha_log);
beta <- exp(beta_log);
gamma <- exp(gamma_log);

Have you plotted your data to see what the relationship between rice[i,j]
and water[i,j] looks like, with and without log transforms?

What's the motivation for using this discontinuous model rather than some
more standard positive-constrained GLM for rice[i,j]? I'd be tempted to
start with something much simpler, like

log(rice[i,j]) ~ normal(xi[i] * water[i,j] + delta[i], sigma);

and draw (delta[i], xi[i]) from a bivariate normal hierarchical prior.

This changes the functional relationships quite a bit, which is why I renamed
the variables to delta and xi, which are now unconstrained. The reason not to
the parameterization beta[i] * (water[i,j] - gamma[i]), even in your original
formulation, is that it's

beta[i] * water[i,j] - beta[i] * gamma[i],

which increases the correlation of the parameters compared to:

xi[i] * water[i,j] + delta[i].

You can always transform back to beta and gamma here given xi and delta.

> where rice[i,j] is the rice harvest for village i in year j (in tons per hectare), water[i,j] is the water (in
> millimeters) applied to the fields during the growing season, and alpha, beta, and gamma are parameters (all greater
> than zero) that characterize, respectively, the maximum yield, the water-use efficiency, and the minimum required water.
> If you supply less water than gamma, your plants die and you get no rice. If you supply more than gamma, then the rice
> harvest increases with water, asymptotically approaching alpha when the water is much greater than gamma. We are
> studying drought and water scarcity, so in many years water is close enough to gamma that we can't ignore it.
>
> The goal of the analysis is to find alpha, beta, and gamma for each village, with estimates of their uncertainty. These
> numbers will then be used in an econometric analysis of the marginal value of changing the supply of water for irrigation.
>
> I'm not sure yet how I want to model the noise (the stochastic variation in rice from year to year if water is held
> constant). The amount of rice has to be greater than or equal to zero, so I could add noise drawn from a distribution
> before applying the max(0, ...) function but maybe there's a more efficient way to do it.

> My student fit the parameters alpha, beta, and gamma for each village individually, using a canned gradient search
> function in Matlab, but some of the villages have short records and never get enough water to clearly observe the
> asymptote at alpha, so the fits are not well constrained. After reading Phil's post at Andrew's blog "Everything I need
> to know about Bayesian statistics, I learned in eight schools
> <http://andrewgelman.com/2014/01/21/everything-need-know-bayesian-statistics-learned-eight-schools/>" I'm thinking that

> this is a lot like his radon in Minnesota problem and it would be better to model the data together, using a
> hierarchical treatment of inter-village variation in alpha, beta, and gamma by drawing each village's parameters from a
> parent distribution, so the villages with lots of data and lots of variation in water can help constrain alpha on the
> villages with short records and/or little variation in water.
>
> However, I am new to MCMC analysis and have some trepidation at diving into Stan with a model that's both nonlinear and
> not continuously differentiable (as the note at the beginning of section 29.5 in the manual warns). Is this problem just
> too pathological, or is it reasonable to try Stan?

You might run into the same problem trying to calculate an MLE,
because the terms drop out of the likelihood, too.

> I am working on coding a model using rstan and generating synthetic data with known alpha, beta, and gamma to see
> whether I can recover the parameters, but I'm new to this and slow, so I figured that I would ask the experts for advice
> in parallel with trying to figure it out on my own.

We'd be happy to comment on concrete model proposals, too.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonlinear model with discontinuous gradient [Ben or Andrew?]
parts: Given

rice[i,j]
= max(0,
alpha[i] * (1 - exp( - beta[i] * (water[i,j] - gamma[i])))

would it be OK to put an upper-bound constraint on gamma[i] so
that it's guaranteed to be less than water[i,j]? Stan's constraint
language doesn't allow a vector to be constrained componentwise, but
you could do the transform yourself.

That is, declare

parameters {
...
real<lower=0,upper=1> gamma_raw;

transformed parameters {
real[I] gamma;
...
for (i in 1:I)
gamma[i] <- gamma_raw[i] * min(water[i]);

That constrains each gamma[i] to run between 0 and min(water[i,j]).
You wouldn't need a prior to make the model proper because gamma_raw
is uniform, or you could include something like a beta prior on
the proportion if that makes sense.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonlinear model with discontinuous gradient [Ben or Andrew?]
parts:
Hi, Bob (and the rest of the list).

After looking carefully at my data, I decided that although the function
I started with is strongly physically motivated, the data itself was way
too unreliable to justify fitting such a difficult function. In
particular, the data near where my gamma parameter would matter most was
not trustworthy (e.g., some sites were reporting large rice yields with
zero water).

If I censor the data and only look at data where the fields get more
than half a meter of water, the data looks much more believable. Also,
the practical policy-relevant questions we're asking deal with the
diversion of large amounts of water to irrigation. This part of the data
is noisy, but believable, and straight linear regression looked like the
better way to go (it's in the asymptotic region of the exponential
formula). I modified the RATS model to make a linear model that would
work with my problem and got things to work nicely.

In the end, the results of the multilevel approach were
indistinguishable from MLE linear fits of each village in isolation, but
the exercise of starting with messy data and a complicated model and
thinking through the most practical way to analyze things was very
useful for me.

The questions you asked and the way you asked them were a lot of help in
getting my mind oriented to getting clear what I was trying to do and
how to approach finding a useful and tractable model. If I get better
data in the future, I may be returning to this model (I am very
interested in the low water conditions near water = gamma), but for now
the data for low water are just not good enough for me to be able to do
anything useful with them.

Also, since this was my first adventure with Stan that went beyond
adapting textbook exercises, I made a bunch of mistakes and found that
the error messages both from the stan --> C++ compiler and the runtime
stan messages were very helpful in identifying and fixing bugs in my
stan model. For inspecting the output and asking whether it made sense,
the diagnostic plots from Xavier Fernández i Marín's ggmcmc package were
very helpful.

I'm grateful to all of you who make stan and related tools, and are
willing to hold a newb's hand on this list.

Best,
Jonathan
